rows: A raccoon has one kind of colour sensor in its eyes, and you have three. It sees brightness without hue, so the picture is grey.
A Virginia opossum also showed only one kind of cone, most sensitive to yellow-green light near 561 nanometres.
The nine-banded armadillo and the sloths have broken copies of genes that every cone needs, so they see with rods alone.
Anteaters have lost the blue-sensitive cone. The Chinese pangolin has lost it too and kept its other cone.
Raccoons, like other carnivores, have a reflecting layer behind the retina, and opossums, like many marsupials, have one within it. We brighten the shadows to suggest it.
No measurement was found for raccoons or opossums. These are our guesses.
docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 raccoon: Sharpness, field and pupil
The picture is grey, weighted toward yellow-green, where the opossum’s single cone is most sensitive. The weights are this app’s own.

src: docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 mole Light and dark: Slonaker; Animal Diversity Web

rows: An eastern mole’s eyes lie under its skin, and its eyelids almost never part enough to let light in.
Its sight goes no further than telling light from dark, so there is no picture here.
A mole finds its way and its food with a touch-sensitive patch at the tip of its nose and a keen sense of smell. Neither reaches a camera.
A grey field of light and shade is the app's way of showing light without an image. The sources give no more than light and dark.

notes.why: Rod-only eyes (armadillos, sloths) would wash out to white in bright day. A new field that compresses highlights; it waits on a source.
The black bear has a cone-dense area centralis (Heyward 2021); kangaroos may have a band. A separate bear entry would draw it once kangaroo topography is sourced.
Mole: the touch screen could light a small patch under the finger in a dark field. It would be an invention.

rows: A domestic pig has two kinds of colour sensor, most sensitive near 439 and 556 nanometres, and you have three. We show colours the way a person with only two kinds sees them.
An American black bear has a blue-sensitive cone and a red-green one, with at least three red-green cones to each blue. Sea otters carry genes for the same pair.
The tammar wallaby, a small kangaroo, has only two kinds of cone. Some other Australian marsupials have a third.
The platypus and echidnas carry genes for two kinds of cone pigment, as most mammals do.
A tammar wallaby resolves about 4.8 cycles per degree, a twelfth of your 60. A western grey kangaroo’s retina could carry about 11. We blur the picture to about 5.
Asian elephants make out a gap of 8 to 11 minutes of arc near the tip of the trunk, about a tenth of your sharpness. One African elephant managed only 48 minutes.
Bears, otters and other carnivores have a reflecting layer behind the retina that gives light a second pass. Pigs and red kangaroos have none, so the shadows are lifted only a little.
No measurement was found for these. We leave the field as your camera gives it and draw a round pupil.
docs/views/sheets/mammal.md#2 mammal: Field of view and pupil
A platypus senses weak electric fields through its bill, down to about 50 millionths of a volt across a centimetre, and can find and avoid objects by them. No phone senses this, so it is left out.
With &draw=rumble and the microphone on, low sounds shake the lower part of the picture, as vibration through the ground reaches a mole. The drawing is the app's.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are an American black bear, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, and the kind for longer wavelengths outnumbers the other at least three to one. If you are a pig, a review lists two kinds for you as well. Nobody has measured the eyes of a kangaroo, but the tammar wallaby, which belongs to the same genus, has two kinds, so you very likely have two.
rows.note: Left out the peak wavelengths (R9 pig, R1 wallaby) since the numbers had no comparison job. Left out the raccoon, which has one cone kind (R6), because it is not a bear, kangaroo or pig.

rows.title: Bears and otters
rows.text: If you are a black bear, your retina has two kinds of color-sensing cell, and the long-wave kind outnumbers the short-wave kind at least 3 to 1. A review's table lists the same two kinds in the ferret, a relative of stoats, weasels and polecats, and in a dog the two pigments peak at about 430 and 555 nanometers. If you are another bear, a weasel or an otter, you very likely have two kinds as well, although nobody has measured the cells of a sea otter or a northern river otter.
rows.note: Left out a measured claim for the Eurasian otter: the R4 quote is cut off before it states the value.

rows.title: Platypus and echidnas
rows.text: If you are a platypus, the back of your eye is mostly rod cells, the kind that work in dim light, with a minority of cone cells that test positive for red-sensing and blue-sensing pigment, so you have two kinds of color-sensing cell where a human has three. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of an echidna, so what you see in color is unknown if you are one. Nobody has measured it in a close relative either.
rows.note: Left out the 550 and 451 nm peaks (R2, R3): the quote names no species and both records carry the same quote, and the row grade lists wavelength as unknown.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bear, a raccoon, a skunk or a hedgehog, and most other mammals in this group are unmeasured too. Where it has been measured, a wild boar and a western gray kangaroo each see about a third of the fine detail a human sees, and a koala sees about a twelfth. Those figures stay with those species.
rows.note: Corrected "grey" to "gray". Kept to three measured species for brevity; the elephant, rhinoceros, hippopotamus and opossum values were left out.

rows.title: Elephants
rows.text: If you are an African bush elephant, you see a little under half the fine detail a human sees. A calculation from how tightly the cells that carry signals out of your retina are packed puts your best sharpness at about 14 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart.
rows.note: Removed the one-word label that was flagged as a fragment. The value is an anatomical estimate (13.16 to 14.37), so the row says it is calculated. No other elephant species has a record.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a Virginia opossum or an African bush elephant, the back of your eye has a tapetum, a light-reflecting layer. A review of eye structure says the pig and the red kangaroo have none. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, and if you are a bear or a gray kangaroo, nobody has described whether you have a tapetum.
rows.note: No record gives dim-light sensitivity for any bear, kangaroo or pig. The pig and red kangaroo statement comes from a review quote filed under the Primates record (R14), so it is kept to those two named animals.

rows.title: Field of view and pupil
rows.text: If you are a wild boar, a Bornean bearded pig or an African elephant, your pupil is round, and if you are a hippopotamus, your pupil is horizontal, wider than it is tall. Nobody has recorded the pupil shape of a bear or a kangaroo, and nobody has measured how wide an area your eyes cover around your head.
rows.note: No field-of-view record exists for any species in this view; the 240 and 271 degree figures (honey possum, ferret) were left out because numbers do not carry between species.

rows.title: Electric sense
rows.text: If you are a platypus, you hunt underwater with your eyes and ears closed, and a review says that organs in the skin of your bill sense electricity and touch, and that you use them to locate prey. If you are a short-beaked echidna, nobody has measured whether you have an electric sense.
rows.note: Only the platypus has a record; no record covers bears, kangaroos, pigs or other mammals, so the row says nothing about them. Replaced "reports" with "says".
